Prey is any living creature that is hunted, caught, and eaten by another creature. That's the heart of the word.

A mouse is prey to a cat. A rabbit is prey to a fox. A fish is prey to a shark. In each case, prey is the one being chased and consumed — the victim, the target, the one in danger.

The creature doing the hunting is called a predator. Prey is always on the other side — the one trying to survive, escape, or avoid being caught.

1. The Literal Meaning — In Nature

In the animal world, prey refers to any animal that another animal hunts for food.

  • A deer is the prey of a wolf.
  • A small bird is the prey of a hawk.
  • A seal is the prey of a killer whale.

Notice that prey is always the weaker or more vulnerable one in this relationship — the one being hunted, not the one hunting.

One important grammar note: prey is almost always used without "a" or "s." You don't say "a prey" or "preys." You simply say "prey," the same way you say "water" or "food" — it's a mass noun.

✅ "The lion spotted its prey."
✅ "Zebras are prey for lions."
❌ "The lion spotted a prey."

However, when you're talking about one specific animal that is being hunted right now, saying "the prey" is perfectly fine — the "the" simply points to that particular animal.

2. The Figurative Meaning — In Human Life

This is where the word gets very interesting and widely used. In everyday language, prey doesn't just mean animals. It refers to any person who is targeted, tricked, taken advantage of, or harmed by someone else.

Think of it this way: just as a lion hunts a defenseless deer, some people "hunt" other people — not physically, but through deception, manipulation, or exploitation.

  • Elderly people are often the prey of scammers who trick them out of their money.
  • Children can become prey to people who wish to harm them.
  • Lonely people are sometimes the prey of manipulative individuals who exploit their loneliness.

In every case, the "prey" is the vulnerable one being targeted by someone with bad intentions.
The Most Important Phrase: "Fall Prey To"

This is the most common phrase built around this word, and you will see it everywhere — in books, newspapers, and everyday speech. It means to become a victim of something, to be caught or harmed by it.

  • "She fell prey to his lies." (She was deceived by his lies — she became his victim.)
  • "Many investors fell prey to the scam." (They were tricked by it.)
  • "Don't fall prey to peer pressure." (Don't let peer pressure control and harm you.)

Notice that "fall prey to" is used for both people and situations — you can fall prey to a person, a disease, a habit, a temptation, or a false belief.

Easy prey means someone (or something) that is especially simple to target, trick, or harm — because they are particularly vulnerable, weak, naive, or defenseless.

  • "Tourists who don't know the local language are easy prey for dishonest taxi drivers."
  • "A limping gazelle is easy prey for a cheetah."

The phrase carries a tone of sadness or unfairness — easy prey is someone who never really had a chance to protect themselves.
"Bird of Prey" — A Special Fixed Phrase

A bird of prey is a specific category of bird — one that hunts and eats other animals. Eagles, hawks, owls, falcons, and vultures are all birds of prey. This is a fixed phrase in English, meaning you'll always hear these exact words together.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

This is subtle but important. The word prey always carries a sense of vulnerability, helplessness, and danger. Prey doesn't choose to be prey. It is made prey by the actions of a more powerful force. This is why the word, even in its figurative use, always evokes sympathy for the person being targeted and blame or suspicion toward the one doing the targeting.

If someone calls a person "prey," they are saying that person was unfairly or dangerously targeted — not that the person did anything wrong.

SituationWho is the "prey"?

In nature, prey = the animal being hunted and eaten.
In human life, prey = the person being targeted, tricked, or harmed.
In phrases, "fall prey to" = to become a victim of something, and "easy prey" = someone who is especially easy to victimize.

The word always signals that someone is on the receiving end of danger — never the one causing it.
